processing: An anthocyanin-rich cultivar processed as green tea, and also used as a food ingredient, including leaf puree in dressings and in drinks whose colour shifts when acid is added.
harvest_season: First flush in spring is the reference picking; anthocyanin figures are given for the first-flush shoots.
appearance_dry: Dark rolled leaf, with a purplish cast expected from its pigment.
appearance_liquor: Coloured by anthocyanin rather than plain yellow-green, and the shade changes when acid such as lemon is added.
appearance_wet: Darker than ordinary green tea leaf, with a purplish tone expected from its pigment.
taste_profile: Few tasting notes are on record; as with other anthocyanin-rich teas, expect a firmer, more astringent cup than ordinary sencha.

brewing.notes: Start with a generic green tea method and keep steeps short. Add a little lemon to watch the colour change.

vintage_note: Usually sold as a speciality product rather than as a named harvest, sometimes in teabags or powder, with no vintage. Treat it as a green tea and use it within about a year of packing.
description:
Sunrouge is a Japanese cultivar bred for colour and composition rather than for classic sencha flavour. It contains an unusually large amount of anthocyanin, the pigment family found in many red and purple plants.

Its first-flush shoots hold far more anthocyanin than Yabukita, by reports about 20 times as much. The pigments include delphinidin 3-galactoside, which is rarely found in green tea.

Taste is not the headline here and specific notes are scarce, so expect more firmness than an ordinary sencha and keep steeps short. The fun comes when you add acid and the colour shifts in the cup.

You will mostly find it in functional or novelty products, and it has appeared as a leaf puree in a dressing and in the colour-changing product Hi no Akane. If you want the same idea from another country, look at Kenyan purple tea.
history:
Sunrouge was developed by the Japanese tea research institute now within NARO in joint work with the Nippon Paper group, and registered in 2011. It was selected from naturally crossed seedlings of the high-anthocyanin breeding line Cha Chukan Bohon No. 6.

Research also notes relatively strong resistance to anthracnose and gray blight, and products based on it reached the market from around 2014.
